done.why: The world told me I'd used all 300 turns. I was shut in the Bank of Zork's Small Room holding the portrait and the zorkmid bills, still trying to work out how to get bank property past the doorways. My own count was a few turns behind, because I fired off a big batch of commands at once in the bank and lost track.

about: It's Zork II, the Wizard of Frobozz, retold with extra descriptive warmth. You get shut into a barrow and go south of a ravine, where a cranky, half-competent wizard who was thrown out of the royal court keeps popping up to cast one-word spells on you. Down there the Empire's lost treasures sit behind old Infocom puzzles: a riddle door, a magic well bucket, Alice-in-Wonderland cakes, a robot, a carousel room, a dragon, and a bank that won't let its property leave. The added text mostly gives hints you can play fair with, plus a quiet creepiness: topiary that moves, frescoes with the hero's face burned off.

moments.note: Going north answered that the barrow door shut behind me, 'You may not recall'. A nice wink at Zork I.
First Wizard visit. 'Feeble!' made me drop the lamp, and his look told me the treasure was all south of the ravine. Funny, and it pointed me somewhere.
The 'convention of wizards' from the Fantasize spell went away when I examined it, and the room 'has the grace to look embarrassed'.
Leaving the gazebo listed the unicorn twice in one room description, once cropping grass and once eating roses.
The topiary animals shift every time I examine one. 'You are nearer the middle than you were.' Properly unsettling.
Saying "a well" got a hollow laugh, but 'answer well' worked. Small parser pickiness.
The bucket description practically spelled out the puzzle (fresh water from the ford, carried in a teapot). Generous without being dull.
The Ferment spell left me drunk on the ravine ledge, so every move went somewhere random until it wore off.
The place mat and letter opener trick at the locked door worked on the first try, because the item descriptions had planted it.
Reading the tiny cake lettering through the poison flask as a magnifier. Then the red cake dried up the pool of tears.
The posts in the Posts Room 'look, now that you think of it, exactly like the legs of a table.' Lovely.
I told the robot to take the red crystal sphere and it just vanished. The robot said it didn't have it, and 'find' couldn't find it. No idea where it went.
I pushed the round button myself despite the HIGH VOLTAGE sign and got fried. Fair enough. The scene with the imprisoned face was a good revival.
After dying, all my gear was scattered and I had to walk back the long way. The lamp started dimming soon after (turn 210).
Once the carousel stopped, its description admitted the passages 'are not quite identical after all'. Nice reward for having been thrown around in there.
Taking the portrait: 'You feel slightly less fireproof, not that it came up.' Ha.
The doorway alarm text explained the bank's logic, and that 'the curtain of light was not built by the same people.'
Walking through the curtain sometimes took me to the Vault, sometimes the Small Room, and once the viewing room. I was still working out the rule when turns ran out.

wished: To find out where the red crystal sphere went after the robot took it, or to get it back.
To get past the dragon. It blocked the north tunnel, and I never got to test whether Fireproof would help before it wore off.
To melt the glacier in the Ice Room, but my matchbook was scattered when I died.
To finish the bank puzzle and get the portrait and bills out.
To find the Wizard's own lair and the unicorn's lady, and to work out what the blue sphere's vision of machinery and muttering meant.
A way to count my turns so the 300-turn cap didn't catch me by surprise.

lines.line: His eye goes to your hands, which hold nothing he values, and he relaxes a little: whatever you have come for, you have not found it yet.
lines.why: It made the Wizard a character and told me where the treasure was, all in one look.

lines.line: It will wait for her. You need not.
lines.why: A gentle way to say 'not this puzzle, not now' without breaking the mood.

lines.line: the Wizard's word put it in the room, and the room, having no say in the matter, let it, and has the grace to look embarrassed about it now.
lines.why: Funniest line in the game, and it made the illusion spells fun to poke at.

lines.line: You are nearer the middle than you were.
lines.why: Real creeping dread in a hedge garden.

lines.line: Whatever it is that makes it go up, it will go up with what is in it and without what is not; that is the whole art of buckets.
lines.why: A hint written as a little proverb.

lines.line: They are turned and polished, and look, now that you think of it, exactly like the legs of a table.
lines.why: The shrinking clicked into place for me.

lines.line: Every face that would tell you who he was has been blackened and cracked by heat, with a thoroughness that looks deliberate, as though the dragons had come by afterwards and had views.
lines.why: Dry humor and a bit of world history packed into scenery.

lines.line: You feel slightly less fireproof, not that it came up.
lines.why: It cheerfully wraps up a spell that turned out to be pointless.

fun.why: Puzzles kept paying off: the riddle, the bucket, the key under the door, the cakes and flask, the robot. The Wizard's spells kept things lively. Lost a point for the long walk back after dying and the sphere that vanished.

engagement.why: As a completionist I always had another exit or object to poke. The carousel, the bank's curtain logic and the dragon kept pulling me on, and the turn cap caught me mid-puzzle.

difficulty.why: The expanded descriptions hint generously (bucket, place mat, flask) so the classic puzzles feel fair. The bank's curtain and wall rules were genuinely hard to read, and my own carelessness (the round button) cost me a lot.

interestingness.why: A faithful classic with a new layer: things that hint at how they're meant to be used, moving topiary, frescoes, a carousel that admits its passages differ, a doorway that explains itself. Some odd moments (the doubled unicorn, the sphere vanishing) blurred it.

prose.why: The added prose is witty, exact and atmospheric, and it sits comfortably next to the original Infocom text without clashing.
